newsitem.title: MEXICO: FORECAST - Carso units paint mixed 1996.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Carso units paint mixed 1996.

text.p: Mexico's Grupo Carso SA is expected to post lackluster 1996 profits after uneven performances from its diverse units, though the overall results might mask healthy improvement in the conglomerate's operating margins, analysts said.

Six industry analysts on average forecast 1996 net earnings of 3.24 pesos per share. Analysts said a direct comparison with 1995 earnings would be misleading because of Carso's spin-off last year of its holdings in Telefonos de Mexico.
Carso is expected to report its 1996 results next week.

A weak domestic economy continued to hurt Carso's cigarette and retail divisions, although its industrial units enjoyed further increases in sales and improvements in operating margins thanks to cost-cutting, analysts said.

"The results will give us a mixed picture depending on which part of the company we are talking about. The consumer-related sector will be under price pressure, but the other divisions did well," said Prabhas Panigrahi, a conglomerate analyst at CS First Boston in New York.
Carso is a conglomerate made up of the Cigatam cigarette the Frisco and Nacobre mining concerns, the Condumex wire company, retailer Sanborns and Corporacion Llantera, a tire supplier.
The fourth quarter is usually Carso's strongest, but analysts said they expected overall sales to be little changed from sales in the third quarter because of a weak domestic economy.

"The company has indicated that Sanborns is not going to do well and may be a bit below expectations. And Cigatam may have already hit bottom but is going to recover very slowly," said Urban Larson, an analyst at Salomon Brothers in Mexico City.

But cost-cutting measures, better capacity use and low copper prices should boost margins at Condumex and Nacobre. Larson forecast that Condumex's margins rose some four percentage points from a year earlier to 19.7 percent. The analyst saw margins at Nacobre at 18.5 percent, up some three percentage points.
Martin Lara at Caspian Research in Mexico City saw Carso's overall 1996 operating margin rising to 21.3 percent from 20.9 percent the previous year.
Many analysts see 1997 as a year of consolidation for Carso, which has not made any recent acquisitions that might provide strong growth.
"They have continually improved their margins, and I expect to see continued improvement," Lara said. "They can also expect to ride the recovery in domestic consumption."
